presentingComplaint: Abdominal distension, confusion and low-grade fever 3 days after discharge; diarrhoea has paradoxically stopped in the last 24 hours.
history: Frail 78-year-old care-facility resident, recently completed a 10-day course of IV piperacillin-tazobactam for a hospital-treated aspiration pneumonia (discharged 4 days ago). Developed profuse watery non-bloody diarrhoea (8-10 stools/day) 2 days after starting antibiotics. Over the last 24 hours stool frequency has dropped sharply and the abdomen has become distended and tense, with worsening lethargy and reduced oral intake. Background: type 2 diabetes, chronic kidney disease (baseline creatinine 1.3 mg/dL), atrial fibrillation on apixaban. No recent travel. This paradoxical cessation of diarrhoea with distension in a septic patient signals evolving ileus/toxic megacolon rather than clinical improvement.
examination: Drowsy, GCS 13, appears toxic and dehydrated. Abdomen grossly distended, tympanitic, diffusely tender with sluggish bowel sounds; no peritonism yet but guarding in lower quadrants. Cool peripheries, prolonged capillary refill. No rash, no focal chest signs.
imaging: CT abdomen/pelvis: diffuse pancolonic wall thickening with mural oedema, 'accordion sign' and pericolic stranding; transverse colon dilated to 7 cm consistent with early toxic megacolon; no free air or perforation.
microbiology: Stool NAAT positive for C. difficile toxin B gene (tcdB) with confirmatory positive stool toxin EIA. Blood cultures pending. No enteric pathogens on multiplex panel.
finalDiagnosis: Fulminant (severe-complicated) Clostridioides difficile infection with early toxic megacolon and septic shock
citations: IDSA/SHEA — Clinical Practice Guidelines for Clostridioides difficile Infection — 2021 (focused update)
ACG — Clinical Guideline: Management of Clostridioides difficile Infection — 2021
Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22e — Clostridioides difficile Infection
stewardship: Fulminant CDI: high-dose oral (or NG) vancomycin 500 mg QID PLUS IV metronidazole 500 mg q8h; add vancomycin retention enema if ileus present. Discontinue the inciting piperacillin-tazobactam. Urgent surgical review for possible colectomy given toxic megacolon. Avoid antimotility agents.
contraindications: Do not give antiperistaltic/antimotility agents (loperamide) — precipitate megacolon
IV vancomycin is ineffective for CDI (no luminal concentration) — must be enteral
Oral metronidazole monotherapy inadequate for fulminant disease
Caution with nephrotoxins given acute kidney injury
edgeCases: Diarrhoea may cease as ileus develops — absence of diarrhoea does NOT exclude CDI and can herald deterioration
Marked leukemoid reaction (WBC >25,000) and rising creatinine define severe/fulminant disease even before megacolon
NAAT positivity alone can reflect colonisation; here toxin EIA positivity plus clinical picture confirms active disease
expectedMaiK: Recent antibiotic exposure plus a toxic, distended abdomen with leukemoid reaction and AKI — even with waning diarrhoea — is fulminant C. difficile infection until proven otherwise.
expectedNextQuestions: Timing and type of recent antibiotic exposure?
Trend of stool frequency versus abdominal distension?
Any prior CDI episodes or proton-pump inhibitor use?
Signs of peritonism or need for urgent surgical assessment?
expectedInvestigations: Stool C. difficile toxin testing (NAAT + toxin EIA, two-step algorithm)
CT abdomen/pelvis to assess colonic dilatation and complications
Serial lactate, WBC, creatinine and albumin for severity staging
Blood cultures and abdominal X-ray to monitor for megacolon/perforation

investigations: Stool C. difficile NAAT and toxin EIA

regressionAssertions: Engine must rank C_DIFF as the top diagnosis despite reduced diarrhoea and prominent distension
Recent antibiotic exposure + leukemoid reaction + AKI must trigger severe/fulminant CDI severity flag
Recommended therapy must be enteral vancomycin (high-dose) plus IV metronidazole, NOT IV vancomycin alone
System must flag toxic megacolon and prompt surgical review
Antimotility agents must be flagged as contraindicated
